crop_profile.summary: Wheat (Triticum aestivum) is a globally important annual cereal grown on loamy to clay soils with pH 6.0-7.5. Optimal temperatures are 10-25 °C, rainfall 300-900 mm/year, and sunlight 6-10 h/day. It requires medium water and nitrogen, with critical moisture needs during flowering. Major producers include China, India, Russia, the United States, and France. Typical yields are 3 t/ha, reaching up to 7 t/ha under optimal management. Key diseases are Fusarium head blight, powdery mildew, and leaf rust; main pests include aphids, Hessian fly, and wheat midge. Integrated pest management, split nitrogen fertilization, and timely harvest ensure high quality grain.

recommendation.recommendation: Apply split nitrogen fertilizer to correct low soil nitrogen levels
recommendation.justification: Soil analysis shows nitrogen is low, which is below wheat's medium requirement and could reduce yield if not corrected. Weather, soil pH, organic carbon, and canopy vigor are all optimal, so addressing the nitrogen deficit now will maximize the existing favorable conditions without added risk.
actions: Confirm current soil nitrogen level with a quick field soil test (if not already done).
Apply the first split of nitrogen fertilizer (≈50 % of the total recommended rate, e.g., 60 kg N/ha as urea) within the next 3 days, incorporating it into the top 10 cm of soil.
Schedule the second split of nitrogen (remaining 50 %) at the tillering stage, roughly 30 days after sowing.
Use a balanced N‑PK formulation if additional phosphorus or potassium is needed, but prioritize nitrogen.
Record the date, rate, and method of each application in the farm log.
recommendation.expected_outcome: Restored soil nitrogen to optimal levels, sustaining the high NDVI canopy, preventing yield loss, and enabling the wheat crop to reach its full yield potential under the current favorable weather and soil conditions.
monitoring_plan: Weekly visual scouting of canopy color and vigor; note any signs of nitrogen deficiency (yellowing of lower leaves).
Measure leaf chlorophyll content with a SPAD meter every 10 days to track nitrogen status.
Re‑sample soil nitrogen 2 weeks after the first application to verify uptake.
If NDVI or SPAD readings drop below healthy thresholds, adjust the second nitrogen split accordingly.
Document all observations and any additional fertilizer adjustments.
